properties.title: Medical world models in healthcare: capabilities, evidence, and trustworthy clinical translation
Medical world models in healthcare: capabilities, evidence, and trustworthy clinical translation

properties.name: Six architecture layers
properties.content: State representation; transition modelling; explicit actions; causal/mechanistic constraints; planning; embodied interaction. Components can be composed and are not universal proof that every cited system implements all layers.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

properties.name: Belief and observation contract
properties.content: Conceptual partially observed formulation separates latent patient state, observation/acquisition process and action-conditioned transition; inference uses available history. Explicit equations are specification only, not an implemented inference engine.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

properties.name: Capabilities versus clinical claims
properties.content: Review L1-L4 framework couples stronger clinical interpretation to increasing causal and clinical evidence. Its L3/L4 claim requirements differ from the project functional capability ontology and must not silently replace it.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

properties.name: Six application domains
properties.content: Imaging, EHR trajectories, disease/response, physiological signals, embodied/procedural systems and population/health systems; digital twins are a crosscutting relationship, not an extra seventh domain.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

properties.name: Clinical translation evidence gates
properties.content: Data completeness/provenance; action specification; causal validity; trajectory uncertainty; external transport; prospective benefit; reproducibility/lifecycle; governance and clinician oversight. Gates are required evidence domains, not passed clinical evidence.
properties.attribution: This paper own taxonomy/recommendation; not an implemented cited system

properties.name: Selection accounting
properties.content: 3528 initial records; prespecified ACM field filter removes1950;1578 remaining minus123duplicates gives1455;1426 screened exclusions leaves29;271 directed/contextual sources gives300. Strict14 are nested within29, not14additional records. Directed additions limit prevalence interpretation.

Figure 1.Literature identification and selection flow. Electronic database searches and the initial seed
set yielded 3,528 records. Following prespecified ACM field filtering, cross-source deduplication, and
two-stage machine-assisted screening with author verification, 29 records were retained after eligibility
assessment. An additional 271 directed contextual, foundational, methodological, and recent sources were
retained through directed searches and bibliography reconciliation, yielding a final narrative corpus of 300
sources, including a strict empirical subset of 14 medical world-model studies. This evidence-mapping
flow is not presented as a PRISMA-ScR diagram.
The final manuscript-aligned narrative corpus therefore comprised 300 unique cited sources
(29+271=300 ). Of the 29 database- or seed-derived cited sources, 14 met the strict empirical definition
of a medical world-model study. Thus, the strict empirical subset was nested within the screened
cited-source set, rather than constituting a separate addition to the 300-source corpus. The remaining

4.7 Architectural evolution of world models
World models have evolved from environmental simulators towards medical dynamic modelling. In 2018,
Ha and Schmidhuber proposed the World Models framework, which used a visual encoder, an
MDN-RNN, and a controller to construct an internally rollable virtual environment15. Dreamer then
adopted and extended RSSM-based latent dynamics for imagined behaviour learning, substantially
improving the efficiency of long-term simulation and planning11, 12, 38, 107. JEPA proposed predictive
representation learning, reducing dependence on pixel-level reconstruction and strengthening high-level
semantic modelling13, 164, 165. Diffusion models further advanced high-fidelity dynamic simulation and
showed potential for medical image generation and disease-course prediction24, 101, 114. The development
of multimodal foundation models and embodied intelligence has pushed world models to integrate vision,
text, physiological signals, and clinical knowledge, forming medical world models that can support
candidate long-term planning under clinical validation1, 2, 16–22. Table 5 compares these major technical
routes and their medical-use boundaries.

5.1 Capability Levels and Claim-Specific Evidence
The L1–L4 framework proposed by Qazi and colleagues provides a useful description of functional
capability51. L1 comprises temporal prediction without an explicit action variable. L2 conditions state
transitions on specified actions. L3 compares predicted outcomes under alternative actions that were not
all observed for the same patient. L4 uses internal rollouts for closed-loop planning or control. To avoid
overstating capability, studies reporting action-conditioned generation without explicit alternative-action
comparison are classified as L2. These levels describe functional scope rather than evidence quality or
clinical maturity. At the final search date of 20

Deployment requires governance mechanisms that remain effective after initial validation. FUTURE-AI
emphasizes trustworthy and deployable clinical AI, including fairness, traceability, robustness, and human
oversight84. These requirements are especially important for world models because errors can propagate

TRIPOD+AI and MI-CLAIM provide foundations for
transparent model reporting83, 85; DECIDE-AI addresses early prospective evaluation within clinical
workflows94; and SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI specify how protocols and trial reports should describe
AI-supported interventions89, 90. Applying these frameworks sequentially helps separate reproducible
technical performance from workflow benefit and, ultimately, patient outcomes.
External validation should include institutions, scanners, documentation practices, and treatment policies
that were not used for development or fine-tuning. Temporal validation is equally important because
clinical practice, coding conventions, and patient populations change. Prospective studies should measure
unsafe recommendations, abstention quality, clinician override, workflow burden, and downstream
outcomes in addition to conventional accuracy. Capability levels such as L1–L4 must remain separate
from evidence maturity: a model can perform closed-loop rollout in a benchmark while still lacking the
validation required for clinical use. Accordingly, increasingly advanced world-model capabilities should
not be interpreted as increasingly strong clinical evidence unless the corresponding validation
requirements are met.
